parts.title: “Listening to the word autism changes everything”: how an autism diagnosis changes a family's life
parts.abstract:
Introduction

When a child is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), the change reaches far beyond a doctor's label. It reshapes a family's feelings, its relationships and the way everyday life is organized. We wanted to understand what this journey feels like from the inside. We carried out a descriptive, exploratory study based on people's own accounts, rather than on measurements. We asked Spanish parents about their experiences and expectations while their child was working through the process of getting a diagnosis. We also asked how the diagnosis affected family life and what parents worried about the future.

Methods

Seventeen parents of children with ASD took part in online interviews. We used a semi-structured format: we had a set of guiding questions, but we could follow up on whatever each parent brought up. Before each parent agreed to take part in writing, we explained how the study would work, that the interview would be recorded, and how we would keep their information private and handle the data. We recorded each interview, typed it out word for word, and studied it using inductive qualitative content analysis. This means we let the main ideas come out of the parents' own words, rather than sorting them into categories we had decided on in advance. We first looked at each interview on its own, as one family's story in its own setting. Then we compared the patterns that parents shared with the ones that differed.

Results

Three big themes came out of the interviews: (1) the impact of the diagnosis and how the family adjusted; (2) the emotional impact, the ways parents coped, and the reorganization of family life; and (3) worries about the future. Parents described a long, uncertain journey to diagnosis. Professionals often did not take their early worries seriously. Their feelings were mixed: shock, sadness and relief all came up at once. Grief and adjustment did not follow a straight line. They came back again and again, as parents had to rethink the expectations they had imagined for their child. Parents coped by leaning on other parents, actively searching for services and for personal assistants, organizing and planning everyday routines, and adjusting their goals to fit their child's abilities. These strategies helped them manage daily demands, but they also took constant watchfulness and a great deal of effort. The diagnosis also deepened the bond between parent and child, affected brothers and sisters, and greatly reorganized family life. Worries about whether the child could become independent, whether care would continue, and whether support would be available as an adult stayed at the center of their concerns.

Discussion

These findings show that families need clear guidance after a diagnosis, lasting emotional support, and services that work together and are built around the family, all the way through the child's life.
parts.introduction_first: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a condition that comes from how the brain develops. It has many sides. It shows up in a wide range of symptoms that deeply affect how people communicate, how they relate to others and how they behave. People with ASD can differ a lot in how the condition presents and in how much help they need (Sánchez Amate and Luque de la Rosa, 2024; World Health Organization (WHO), 2025). Over recent decades, more and more children have been diagnosed with ASD, so it has become more and more important for public health and for society. Around the world, the share of children with ASD is thought to be rising, at about 0.77% of all children (Issac et al., 2025). In Spain, this rise is easy to see in schools. More than 90,000 students there have been diagnosed with ASD, and that number has kept growing in recent years (Autismo España, 2026).
parts.conclusion:
5

Conclusions

Parents' stories suggest that an ASD diagnosis can deeply reshape everyday family life. For many, the journey to diagnosis was a hard transition. It brought a long period of uncertainty, professionals often did not take parents' early worries seriously, and getting the right support for the child took time.

Without proper guidance after the diagnosis, parents described their roles growing much bigger. They went beyond the usual duties of raising a child to become their child's voice, the people who organized support, and experts on what their child needed. This change could strengthen the bond between parent and child and help the family adapt. But it also meant carefully organizing routines, sharing parents' time and attention among brothers and sisters, and leaving less room for family life to be spontaneous or for the family to take part in social activities.

Parents' biggest worry was about the future: whether their child could become independent, whether care would continue, and whether services would be available as an adult. These findings support the need for policies and services that look after not only the child with ASD, but also parents' emotional wellbeing and the way the wider family works. Health care, education and social care services should work together and keep supporting families throughout the journey to diagnosis and through the next big steps in the child's life.
parts.introduction_rest:
This rise in diagnoses does not only come from better screening and better ways of diagnosing. It also reflects that people are more aware of autism, and that the rules doctors use to decide who has it have changed (Centers for Disease Control Prevention (CDC), 2023). But a diagnosis is about more than numbers. It is a deeply life-changing event for families. It is not just a medical label. It breaks into the story of the parents' lives, changing what they expected, who they felt they were, and how they organized their days (Boss, 1999; Woodgate et al., 2008; Dounavi and Koldas, 2025). Health care usually focuses on the child who gets the diagnosis. Yet its effects spread to the whole family, changing relationships between family members and parents' emotional wellbeing (Sánchez Amate and Luque de la Rosa, 2024).

Spotting autism early is essential, because it lets help start on time. In real life, though, the time between when parents first suspect something is wrong and when their child gets a formal diagnosis of a neurodevelopmental disorder (a condition that affects how the brain develops) is often far too long (Daniels et al., 2021; Dounavi and Koldas, 2025). Researchers describe this journey as a "biographical disruption": a break in the family's story. Families start in a phase of uncertainty, noticing early signs. Then comes the moment the diagnosis is confirmed, and after that they reorganize their lives (Edwards et al., 2018; García-Bravo et al., 2023; Dounavi and Koldas, 2025). Along the way, parents run into many barriers built into the system. They wait a long time for a diagnosis, they get little guidance from institutions, and they find it hard to reach specialists. Together, these problems have been called a "diagnostic odyssey", a long and winding journey to a diagnosis (Creswell and Poth, 2018; Centers for Disease Control Prevention (CDC), 2023, 2025). In this study, when we talk about health and social-care support, we mean the health care, education, community and social services that families use while their child is working through the diagnosis, through childhood, and as the child moves into adulthood.

In earlier studies, parents described the journey as a "tortuous path", a winding, difficult road. Some health professionals, especially in primary care (the first point of contact, such as a family doctor), tended to play down the first symptoms. Parents then had to keep fighting to be heard and to get answers (Garcia-Bravo et al., 2025). In Spain, these problems are made worse by delays in getting diagnostic tests and by the small number of services in the public health system. Many families end up paying for private health care. All of this causes a lot of stress and emotional strain. It directly affects parents' mental wellbeing and, indirectly, the child's development (Sánchez Amate and Luque de la Rosa, 2024).

Caregiving, the work of looking after and supporting a child, should not be thought of as starting only once the diagnosis is confirmed. Before that, parents may already be watching their child closely, asking for help again and again, and making small, informal changes to cope with differences in how their child is developing, even though nobody has explained them yet. So the diagnosis may matter less as the moment caregiving begins than as a moment of rethinking. It can confirm parents' earlier worries, reshape their expectations, and turn their efforts toward official help, finding services, speaking up for their child, and planning for the long term (Edwards et al., 2018; García-Bravo et al., 2023; Dounavi and Koldas, 2025). For this reason, we should see caregiving as something that changes across three periods: before the diagnosis, during the diagnosis, and after the diagnosis. It is not simply a split into "before" and "after".

The emotional impact of learning that a child has a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition does not stop at one reaction, now or later. Instead, parents may go through a changing process of grief and adjustment. It can include shock, disbelief, uncertainty, sadness, guilt, and searching for explanations. In some cases, it ends with relief, because parents finally have a way to make sense of how their child is developing (Edwards et al., 2018; García-Bravo et al., 2023). These feelings are not fixed, they do not happen the same way to everyone, and they do not always come one after another. Parents may move back and forth between them, feel several at the same time, or feel them again at different points in their child's life. For ASD, this process has been linked to what is called "ambiguous or non-finite grief". This is not grief over losing the child. It is grief over the change in the expectations parents had imagined for their child's development, for family life and for the future (Boss, 1999; O'Brien, 2007; Bravo-Benítez et al., 2019; Mihandoust et al., 2021). Feelings of loss and uncertainty may come back again and again. This can happen during big steps in the child's development, when the child is compared with other children, when expectations are not met, or when parents worry about whether their child will be able to look after themselves and get support in the future. This pattern is similar to what is called "chronic sorrow", a lasting, recurring sadness, and it shows that parents keep having to adjust (Coughlin and Sethares, 2017).

At the same time, ASD may bring big changes to how a family works. Roles may be shared out differently, everyday routines may be reorganized, the bond between parent and child may grow stronger, brothers and sisters may be affected, and in some cases the family may become cut off from others because of stigma, the unfair negative judgment people can feel toward someone with a condition (Sánchez Amate and Luque de la Rosa, 2024; Garcia-Bravo et al., 2025). At first, parents may feel overwhelmed and not ready enough to decide on treatments and other kinds of help. But they can slowly learn from experience and move from the usual role of a parent to becoming their child's voice and experts on what their child needs (Edwards et al., 2018). This change does not necessarily mean the grief is over. Instead, it is an ongoing process of fitting the diagnosis into family life while parents keep adjusting their expectations and the ways they care for their child.

How a family adjusts after an ASD diagnosis also depends on the strategies parents use to handle its emotional, practical and relationship demands. Coping includes actions, changes in relationships, and changes in how parents make sense of things. Examples are looking for information and support from others, reorganizing everyday routines, speaking up for the child, and rethinking earlier expectations. Helpful strategies, especially support from other people and "positive reappraisal" (looking at a situation in a more positive way), have been linked to caregivers feeling better and being less emotionally distressed (Sánchez Amate and Luque de la Rosa, 2024). Still, how well a strategy works depends on the situation. Its usefulness may change with the family's circumstances, the resources they have, and how much support the child needs.

A family systems view sees the family as a set of relationships in which members depend on each other. A change in one member affects how the whole family works, the roles people play, and the relationships between them (Cox and Paley, 1997; Rogers et al., 2022). The smaller groups within a family, such as parents together or parents and children, affect each other in both directions. They keep adjusting to changes inside the home and in the wider world around them (Rogers et al., 2022). An ASD diagnosis may therefore call for changes in relationships between parents and children and between brothers and sisters. These include sharing care duties differently, reorganizing time and attention, and reworking roles and boundaries that were set before. Parents may go beyond the usual role of a parent to become their child's voice, the people who organize support, and the people who explain what their child needs. Brothers and sisters may notice changes in how much attention they get from their parents, in what the family expects of them, and in the responsibilities they may be expected to take on in the future. All of this happens while parents face the gap between the family life they had imagined and their child's real needs for development and support.

Alongside the demands of daily life, worries about the future are a central part of families' experiences. Parents especially worry about whether their child can become independent, whether support will be available as an adult, and whether care will continue (Garcia-Bravo et al., 2025; Autismo España, 2024). These worries grow when families feel that support shrinks once the child leaves school. This shows why we need to understand families' experiences in depth, looking at the whole picture (Autismo España, 2024; Issac et al., 2025).

Qualitative research, which studies people's experiences through their own words and accounts, is especially useful for understanding complicated processes from the point of view of the people who live through them. It can also uncover the beliefs, values and reasons behind how people make health choices (Carpenter and Suto, 2008; Moser and Korstjens, 2017; Korstjens and Moser, 2017). Within this kind of research, descriptive, exploratory studies let us look at experiences of illness and disability in real-life settings, taking people's own views into account within their own social surroundings (Bradshaw et al., 2017; Jack and Phoenix, 2022). In this study, we understand "lived experience" as the personal, situation-dependent way in which parents see, understand and give meaning to their child's journey to diagnosis and to what it means for everyday family life (Neubauer et al., 2019). These experiences are shaped by the child's characteristics and support needs, by who is in the family, by what parents expected before, by the resources available, and by how the family deals with health care, education, community and social-care services. So we do not assume that every family goes through the diagnosis in the same way. Instead, we treat each parent's account as its own story, set within a particular family and social situation. This lets us respect how unique each parent's experience is, while still finding patterns that parents share and patterns that differ.

Even though interest in ASD is growing, more qualitative research is needed to explore parents' lived experiences in depth, while recognizing that each experience and each family is different. Understanding these experiences is essential for designing help that is built around the family, for public policies, and for ways of providing care.

The aim of this study was to explore the lived experiences and expectations of Spanish parents of children with ASD while their child was working through the diagnosis. We also wanted to learn how parents saw the diagnosis affecting everyday family life, family relationships, and their worries about the future.
parts.methods:
2

Materials and methods

2.1

How we designed the study

We carried out a descriptive, exploratory study based on people's own accounts, following well-established ways of doing this kind of research (Jack and Phoenix, 2022; Bradshaw et al., 2017). We followed two international guidelines for reporting this kind of research, called COREQ (Tong et al., 2007) and SRQR (O'Brien et al., 2014). Both are promoted by the EQUATOR Network, a group that helps researchers report their work clearly.

Research based on people's own accounts is especially good for studying complicated situations from the point of view of the people living through them. It lets us look closely at what health experiences mean to people, what they believe, and what in their surroundings shapes those experiences (Carpenter and Suto, 2008; Moser and Korstjens, 2017). With this approach, we could explore parents' experiences of disability and of getting a diagnosis in real-life settings, while taking into account the families and communities they lived in (Bradshaw et al., 2017; Jack and Phoenix, 2022).

We focused on what Spanish parents of children with ASD expected and went through while their child was working through the process of getting a diagnosis. We also asked how they saw the diagnosis affecting everyday family life. We worked from a "lived-experience" point of view. This means we treated each parent's story as their own personal view, shaped by their situation and by their particular family and social surroundings. So we looked at each parent's account on its own, not at stories told by two parents together or by the whole family.

2.2

Who took part

2.2.1

How we chose people and how many

We chose people on purpose, picking those who had direct and relevant experience linked to what we wanted to study. This is called purposive sampling (Creswell and Poth, 2018; Carpenter and Suto, 2008). To make it easier to find people, we also used snowball sampling: the first parents we interviewed suggested other parents who might fit.

In this kind of research, the number of people is not decided by statistics about how well a group represents a larger population. Instead, it is decided by "data saturation": the point where new interviews stop bringing up new ideas (Creswell and Poth, 2018; Moser and Korstjens, 2018). Earlier studies suggest that saturation usually comes between nine and 17 interviews. In more structured studies, it can take longer, up to 15–23 interviews (Hennink and Kaiser, 2022; Squire et al., 2024).

2.2.2

Who could take part and who could not

We set rules for who could take part, so that everyone in the group was suitable for the topic. Parents were included if they: (a) were parents of a child with a medical diagnosis of ASD, (b) had a child enrolled in a school in Spain that follows an inclusive approach, meaning it welcomes and supports children with special needs alongside other children, (c) had recent and ongoing experience with the education system (at least during the last school year), and (d) spoke Spanish well enough to take part in the interviews and to give informed consent. Informed consent means a person agrees to take part after being told what the study involves.

Parents were left out if they: (a) did not actively take part in their child's education, (b) had barriers that stopped them from taking part, or (c) did not give informed consent, or later took it back, at any stage of the study.

2.2.3

How we invited people

We shared an invitation through the autism associations and inclusive schools that worked with us. The invitation briefly explained what the study was for, who could take part, that taking part was voluntary, how the interviews would work, and how to contact the research team. Staff from these organizations did not tell us the names or contact details of the parents who might be interested.

Parents who wanted to take part contacted the research team directly. We invited them to a first information session, where we explained the study's goals, how it would work and what was needed to take part. We also asked the parents who joined to pass the invitation on to other parents who might fit, as part of the snowball sampling. These parents also had to contact the research team directly, and we did not give them any contact details of other people.

Parents who agreed to take part received an information sheet and an informed consent form by email. Once they had given their written consent, we set up the interview and sent them the details for the online session.

2.2.4

How we collected the information

We held one interview with each parent, so there were 17 interviews in total. Each was semi-structured, meaning we had guiding questions but could follow up on what each parent said. The interviews lasted between 40 and 80 minutes and took place online through Microsoft Teams, which let us explore each parent's experiences in depth.

We wrote an interview guide with a set of topics. We based these topics on the work of Gallego-Jiménez et al. (2025) and adjusted them to fit our study's goal and the parents taking part. The guide used open-ended questions, which cannot be answered with a simple "yes" or "no", and flexible follow-up prompts to explore new things that came up in each parent's story. Table 1 shows the main guiding questions and the topics we covered. Two members of the research team, G.M.G.J. and S.T.-M., both university researchers with earlier experience in semi-structured interviews, carried out all the interviews. The interviewer had no previous relationship with the parents.

Table 1

Interview guide.

| Main topic | What we explored | Main guiding question and possible follow-up questions

| The journey to diagnosis | First worries, contact with professionals, the moment the diagnosis was confirmed | Main guiding question: Can you tell me about the process from the moment you first became concerned about your child's development until the diagnosis was confirmed? Possible follow-up questions: What first caught your attention? How did professionals respond to your worries? Were there any delays, difficulties or turning points along the way?

| The impact of the diagnosis | Feelings, what the diagnosis meant, changes in expectations | Main guiding question: How did you experience the moment when the diagnosis was told to you, and what did the diagnosis mean to you at that time? Possible follow-up questions: What thoughts or feelings did you have? Did receiving the diagnosis change how you understood your child's development? Did it change your expectations for your child or your family life?

| Guidance and support | Information received, access to resources, support from institutions | Main guiding question: What information, guidance or support did you receive during and after the journey to diagnosis? Possible follow-up questions: Did you know what steps to take after the diagnosis? Which professionals, organizations or other parents helped you? What information or support did you feel was missing?

| How the family adjusted | Ways of coping, acceptance, how the parents' role changed over time | Main guiding question: How have you and your household adapted to your child's needs throughout the journey to diagnosis? Possible follow-up questions: Has your role as a parent changed? What strategies have helped you cope or adapt? Have your priorities, goals or expectations changed over time?

| Daily life | Routines, organizing the day, changes in lifestyle | Main guiding question: Can you describe how everyday family life is currently organized around your child's needs? Possible follow-up questions: What role do routines and planning play? How do you handle unexpected situations or changes? Have outings, free-time activities or social relationships been affected?

| Family relationships | Relationship between parent and child, effect on brothers and sisters, relationships within the family | Main guiding question: How do you see your child's needs and the journey to diagnosis having affected relationships and responsibilities in your household? Possible follow-up questions: Has your relationship with your child changed? How is time, attention and responsibilities shared? How do you think brothers and sisters or other family members experience the situation?

| Emotional burden | Stress, related feelings, mental wellbeing | Main guiding question: How has this experience affected you emotionally over time? Possible follow-up questions: Have your feelings changed since your first worries or the diagnosis? Are there feelings or worries that come back at certain moments? What situations are hardest on you emotionally right now?

| Looking ahead | Independence, long-term worries | Main guiding question: What are your main hopes and worries about your child's future? Possible follow-up questions: What does independence mean for your child in their particular situation? What worries you about future care? How do you imagine your child's life as a teenager and as an adult?

| Support systems | Resources as an adult, inclusion in society and work | Main guiding question: What support does your child receive now, and what support do you think will be needed in the future? Possible follow-up questions: How would you describe how well services work together? What worries you about the end of compulsory schooling? What resources, job opportunities or community support do you think are missing right now?

| Overall reflections | What was learned, what is needed | Main guiding question: Looking back on the journey, what have you learned and what do you think professionals or services should do differently? Possible follow-up questions: What would have helped you during the journey to diagnosis? What advice would you give to professionals supporting other parents? Is there anything important we have not talked about?

Source: prepared by the author.

We used the topics in the guide to explore each parent's experiences in a broad and orderly way, in line with our study's goal. The topics helped shape the information we gathered, but we did not plan them in advance as categories for sorting the answers. Because the format was semi-structured, parents could bring up experiences that belonged to different topics, and the interviewer could change the order of the questions and how deeply to explore each one to suit each story.

During and right after each interview, the interviewer wrote field notes. These noted the setting of the interview, any feelings or body language the parent showed during the online session, interruptions or technical problems, and first impressions of the parent's story. We used these notes to help us understand the written interviews when we analyzed them (Carpenter and Suto, 2008).

While we were sorting and grouping the answers, the members of the analysis team also kept reflexive journals. These were personal records of the researchers' own assumptions, their reactions to the answers, the choices they made in the analysis, disagreements about how to sort answers, and changes they made as they built categories and themes. We reviewed these journals in research-team meetings, to check how our own views might have influenced the analysis and to make sure our decisions were open and clear. We used the journals to understand the setting of the research and to reflect on it, not as information from the parents (Carpenter and Suto, 2008).

We also used member checking, which means going back to the parents to check what we had understood. Any later contact for this was only to confirm or clarify what we had learned, and we did not count it as an extra research interview.

We collected basic information about each parent, such as age, gender, job and number of children. Parents also told us about their child with ASD, including the child's age, gender and the level of support they reported. We did not collect the year or date of the diagnosis as a standard piece of information about each parent.

2.2.5

How we handled the information and kept it private

Before giving informed consent, parents received information in writing and out loud about the study. We told them what the study was for, that taking part was voluntary, that the interviews would be recorded, that we would use quotes with names removed in scientific publications, how we would protect their privacy, how we would store and keep the information, and that they could leave the study at any time without giving a reason. We also told them they could ask for their information to be removed until the written interviews had been made anonymous and added to the combined analysis.

We gave each parent a code made of letters and numbers, from P1 to P17. Each code stood for one person, not a whole family. We kept information that could identify people separate from the interview information. Right after each interview, we moved the recording to a secure, encrypted, password-protected server at our university and deleted it from Microsoft Teams. Only the research team could see the recordings, the written interviews with names replaced by codes, the field notes and the files in ATLAS.ti, a computer program for organizing and labeling research text. We checked every quote we used in publications to remove names and any other details that could reveal who it came from.

2.2.6

How we analyzed the information

We used inductive qualitative content analysis, following Graneheim and Lundman (2004), Graneheim et al. (2017) and Lindgren et al. (2020). In simple terms, we read the interviews closely and let the main ideas come out of the parents' own words. We focused mainly on what the parents said directly: their experiences, events, worries and meanings. This is called manifest content. As we built categories and themes, we also looked at latent content, which means the deeper meanings, tensions and patterns that ran across the parents' stories. We did this at the level of categories and themes, and we always stayed grounded in the words and setting of each interview.

Because we let the ideas come out of the parents' words, we did not use the topics in the interview guide as a fixed set of categories to sort the answers into. Instead, we built codes, categories and themes from the interviews themselves. A code is a short label for an idea in the text. We started with open coding, which means labeling pieces of text with whatever label seemed to fit. Then we compared the labels and grouped them into broader ideas. So something a parent said under one topic could end up in more than one category or theme, and something related could come from different topics and still end up in the same theme (Graneheim and Lundman, 2004; Elo and Kyngäs, 2008; Hsieh and Shannon, 2005; Lindgren et al., 2020).

Each parent was one person in the study, and we analyzed each interview as one parent's account in its own family and social setting. Only then did we compare the patterns parents shared with the ones that differed. We did not analyze two parents together or the whole family. We did not collect the year or date of the diagnosis as a standard piece of information about each parent, so we did not know how long it had been since the diagnosis. We therefore could not use this to choose people, to group them, or to compare them. The study was cross-sectional, meaning it looked at one moment in time, and it was not designed to follow changes over time.

Parents did talk about their worries before the diagnosis, the moment it was confirmed, how they adjusted afterwards, and their worries about the future. But these came up within each parent's story during the interview. We treated them as part of the setting of each account, not as proof that all parents went through the same timeline. Research that follows change over time, called qualitative longitudinal research, builds time into its goals, the choice of people, the way information is collected and the way it is analyzed. It usually collects information again and again at several points in time, which we did not do (Audulv et al., 2022). In line with inductive qualitative content analysis, our final analysis therefore focused on patterns that made sense across the parents' accounts, rather than forcing the answers into a simple split between "before the diagnosis" and "after the diagnosis" (Graneheim et al., 2017; Lindgren et al., 2020).

We typed out each interview word for word. We then picked out meaning units, which are stretches of text that carry one complete idea, such as a sentence or a paragraph. We shortened these and gave each one a descriptive code. Next, we compared the codes and grouped them into categories based on how similar their ideas were. When building themes, we looked at the wider meanings and tensions that linked these categories, while keeping them connected to the original interviews.

In line with inductive qualitative content analysis, we built themes and subthemes from the meaning, setting and importance of the coded text, not by counting how often each code or quote appeared. We treated a subtheme as a smaller part of a theme. When a subtheme came up in several interviews, that was one sign that the experience was shared. But we did not set a number of interviews in advance that a subtheme had to reach to count as valid or important. We kept a possible subtheme when it made sense as an idea, was relevant to our study's goal, was different from the subthemes next to it, and could be traced back to the original meaning units. We could also keep subthemes that came up less often, when they showed a meaningful difference or helped us understand parents' experiences more fully (Hsieh and Shannon, 2005; Elo and Kyngäs, 2008; Graneheim et al., 2017; Lindgren et al., 2020; Sandelowski, 2001).

Two researchers coded the written interviews separately and then compared their first labels. A third researcher reviewed the shared table of codes and took part in discussions about differences in coding, building categories and building themes. The three researchers settled differences by talking them through until they agreed. We held regular analysis meetings to record our decisions and improve the categories and themes. We used ATLAS.ti software (version 26) to organize the written interviews, add and find codes, group related codes, and keep a clear link between each coded meaning unit and the place it came from in the original text. The software helped us organize, find and record the information, but it did not replace our own work of understanding the answers or create categories and themes for us (Vignato et al., 2022). The research team made all coding decisions, built all categories and themes, and did this through repeated comparison, open discussion and agreement.

The written interviews were the main information from the parents. We read the field notes alongside each written interview to understand the setting of the interview, the feelings the parent showed during the online session, interruptions and other details that could help us understand the parent's account. When the field notes added context or suggested a different way of understanding something, we discussed this in research-team meetings.

We did not analyze the reflexive journals as information from the parents. Instead, we used them to record our assumptions, our reactions to the answers, our coding decisions, our disagreements and the changes we made while building categories and themes. These records helped us discuss our own views openly and gave a clear record of how we reached our conclusions.

We chose quotes to show our findings because they were complete in meaning, clear in setting and relevant to our understanding, not just because they were long. In line with qualitative content analysis, a meaning unit can be a word, a sentence or a paragraph, as long as the pieces are connected by their content and setting. So we kept short quotes when they formed a complete idea on their own and were clearly placed within the explanation around them. We used longer passages when we needed more context to show a more complicated experience, or to make clear who or what the parent was talking about, when they were speaking, or what they meant (Graneheim and Lundman, 2004; Eldh et al., 2020).

We translated the quotes from Spanish into English and checked them against the original written interviews, so that their meaning stayed the same.

2.2.7

How we made sure the study was trustworthy

We checked the quality of our methods using four standards set out by Lincoln and Guba (1985): credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.

Credibility means that the findings are believable and true to the parents' experiences. We supported it mainly through researcher triangulation, which means several researchers checking each other's work. Three researchers took part in the analysis, compared their codes and discussed different understandings in regular meetings until they agreed.

The written interviews were the main information from the parents, and the field notes were extra material that helped us understand and improve our reading of each account. Because all the information came from semi-structured interviews, we saw this as several researchers checking each other and combining extra context, not as using several different research methods. We also used member checking to confirm or clarify what we had learned in the interviews.

Transferability means that others can judge whether our findings might apply to their own situation. We supported it by describing in detail the setting of the study, the parents, how we chose them, how we collected the information and how we analyzed it. Dependability means that the analysis is careful and can be followed. We strengthened it through an outside check by a researcher who had not taken part in the first round of coding. This researcher reviewed our research plan, our analysis steps and how we built the categories and themes.

Confirmability means that the findings come from the parents' accounts rather than from the researchers' own views. We supported it through the reflexive journals, which recorded our assumptions, our reactions to the answers and our analysis decisions. We reviewed these journals in team meetings to check how our own views might have affected the coding and the building of themes. Table 2 shows the steps we used to make sure the study was trustworthy (Korstjens and Moser, 2018).

Table 2

How we checked the quality of the study.

| Standard | What we did

| Credibility (believability) | Researcher triangulation: Three researchers took part in the analysis, compared their codes and discussed different understandings until they agreed. Combining extra context: We read the field notes alongside the matching written interviews to understand and improve our reading. Member checking: We contacted parents to confirm or clarify what we had learned in the interviews.

| Transferability (applicability to other situations) | We described in detail the setting of the study, the parents, how we chose them, how we collected the information and how we analyzed it.

| Dependability (careful, followable analysis) | An outside researcher who had not taken part in the first round of coding reviewed our research plan, our analysis steps and how we built the categories and themes.

| Confirmability (findings come from the parents' accounts) | We used reflexive journals to record our assumptions, our reactions to the answers, our coding decisions and the changes we made while building categories and themes. We reviewed these records in research-team meetings.

Source: prepared by the author.

The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki, a set of ethical rules for research involving people. The Ethics Committee of CEU San Pablo University approved it (code: 401.998). All parents gave written informed consent before taking part. Before giving consent, we explained how the interviews would be recorded, how we would protect their privacy, how we would replace their names with codes, how we would store the information, who could see it, how we would use quotes with names removed, and their right to leave the study.
parts.results:
3

Results

Seventeen parents of children diagnosed with ASD took part in our study. Most of them were mothers (88.24% of the parents), and the rest were fathers (11.76%). They were between 32 and 51 years old, with an average age of 45.5. Their education varied quite a lot. About 65% had a university degree, around 25% had studied beyond university, and the remaining 10% had finished vocational training or secondary school.

When it came to work, 55% of the parents worked in education, social care or health care. The other 45% worked in offices, shops and businesses, technology, or other services. In terms of how long they had worked, 40% said they had more than 15 years of experience, 35% had between 5 and 15 years, and 25% had less than 5 years. So the group included both long-established professionals and people early in their careers.

Most parents (76.47%) said they had 2 children, and families had anywhere from 1 to 3 children. The child with ASD was most often the second child born (47.06% of the children with ASD). Some were only children, and others were born before or after their brothers and sisters. In two cases, the child with ASD was a twin, and both twins had been diagnosed.

Among the children with ASD, there were more boys (73.33%) than girls (26.67%). The DSM-5 is the main handbook doctors use to diagnose mental health conditions. It sorts people with ASD into levels of support, from level 1 (least support needed) to level 3 (most support needed). Of the children with ASD, 41.18% were at level 1, 29.41% at level 2 and 29.41% at level 3. This suggests the children were spread fairly evenly across the levels, with a fairly balanced mix of support needs.

Our interview guide covered ten broad areas of questions. Even so, when we let the main ideas come out of the parents' own words, three big themes appeared. The ten areas helped us gather a wide range of information, but they did not decide how we organized what we found. Several areas ended up in the same theme, and some areas fed into more than one theme.

We present the findings by theme, not in a straight line through time. Parents often looked back on several moments in their lives: their first worries, the moment the diagnosis was confirmed, the ongoing process of adjusting, and worries about the future. These moments came from the stories parents told in the interviews. We did not measure how much time had passed since the diagnosis. The moments also often overlapped, and not every family had gone through them in the same order. So we point out changes over time within and across themes only where parents' accounts supported them. We chose this way of presenting the findings to keep the structure that came out of the parents' words, and to tell the story clearly. It is not meant to rebuild a before-and-after comparison of life before and after the diagnosis, which was not part of how we designed the study (Sandelowski, 1998).

Three main themes came out of the analysis: (1) the impact of the diagnosis and how the family adjusted; (2) the emotional impact, the ways parents coped, and the reorganization of family life; and (3) worries about the future (see Figure 1). Each theme is split into smaller subthemes. These are patterns that made sense together and mattered for our analysis, and that we found across parents' accounts. We built them from what the parents' words meant, the setting they came from and how important they were, not just from how often they came up. The quotes we give are examples chosen from all the material we had sorted and labeled. They do not show how many pieces of meaning supported each subtheme. Each quote is labeled with a code from P1 to P17, which stands for one parent. These codes refer to individual parents, not to a family account built together by the whole family.

Figure 1

The themes and subthemes that came out of the analysis, shown as a tree with the big themes at the top and the smaller subthemes below.

3.1

Theme 1: The impact of the diagnosis and how the family adjusted

3.1.1

Subtheme 1.1: First worries and the moment the diagnosis was confirmed

Parents described an early period when they noticed signs that worried them, such as their child not responding when they called his name or not making eye contact. They described this as a kind of "intuitive hyper-vigilance": a sharp, gut feeling that something was wrong. Parents saw these signs as a warning that "something was not right":

"We started to notice that something wasn't as we expected because he didn't respond when we called him" (P1).

Parents noticed that health professionals did not always agree with these early worries. Sometimes they put the difficulties down to normal differences in how children develop. Answers like these made the period of uncertainty last longer. During that time, parents kept noticing differences in their child's development but got no clear explanation:

"The pediatrician said it was developmental delay" (P4).

The diagnosis often came after a long time of uncertainty, and parents described it as a major emotional turning point. At first, they felt shock, sadness and difficulty taking in what the diagnosis meant:

"When they finally confirmed the diagnosis, it was a very hard blow" (P8).

In some accounts, this first shock came together with a feeling of relief, because parents finally had an explanation for the differences they had seen in their child's development. Relief did not remove the distress. Instead, both feelings could happen at the same time, which shows how mixed the experience of getting a diagnosis can be.

Parents' stories suggested that grief and adjustment did not follow one fixed path. Parents moved back and forth between uncertainty, emotional pain, searching for explanations, worrying about the future, and slowly changing what they expected. So their grief was not about losing their child. It was about having to rethink the expectations they had imagined for their child's development, for their independence and for family life:

"Hearing the word autism completely changes how you see your child's future" (P9).

Looking back on their experiences, some parents described a shift toward better understanding and acceptance of their child's own way of developing. But this adjustment did not always mean that sadness or uncertainty disappeared. Worries could come back when the child reached new stages of development or when new support would be needed.

3.1.2

Subtheme 1.2: Feeling lost in the system after the diagnosis

After getting the diagnosis, parents said they often received little guidance or support from services. They described this moment as especially hard emotionally.

"You go home with the diagnosis and you say "Now what?" (P11).

Parents got no clear, organized information about what help was available, what support they could get, or what steps to take next. This left them unsure and searching for help on their own, often by talking to other families:

"Nobody tells you what steps to take" (P2).

"You find out by talking to other families" (P1).

Some parents also looked back on earlier experiences, when they had had to take more of the lead themselves to get services or an assessment.

"Years ago, they gave you the diagnosis and then you were on your own" (P15).

Parents saw this as a lonely search through a complicated system that was hard to get into.

3.1.3

Subtheme 1.3: Changing what parents expected

Looking back on their experiences, parents described how their expectations changed. They moved away from wanting their child to be "normal" and toward accepting their child's own way of developing. This meant rethinking what counted as an achievement, and what goals and targets they set for their child's development. Parents also stressed how important it was to value progress that might seem small to others:

"You learn to value advances that seem small to others" (P14).

"Our dreams and expectations for his development have changed" (P3).

Parents tended to adjust their expectations to match their child's pace, so that neither the child nor the parents would feel frustrated:

"We try not to set rigid expectations; we adapt from day to day" (P8).

"If he points to the pictogram to tell me he wants something, that's enough for me" (P9).

These accounts suggest that parents adjusted by rethinking their expectations and valuing more the progress that helped their child in real life and the meaningful achievements of everyday life.

Across these subthemes, getting the diagnosis was not just about finding out that a child had a medical condition. It was also about reorganizing what parents made sense of. Looking back, parents reinterpreted their earlier worries and began to rebuild the expectations they had imagined for their child's development, independence and future family life.

3.2

Theme 2: The emotional impact, the ways parents coped, and the reorganization of family life

3.2.1

Subtheme 2.1: A stronger bond

Parents described a stronger bond with their children. They became more involved in their care, and the relationship was built on a lot of protection and meeting the child's needs. This bond is built day by day, through being constantly present and taking a direct part in the child's routines, care and development:

"A different, stronger connection is formed with your child with ASD" (P12).

"It is a bond of protection and resilience" (P15).

Parents took on roles that went beyond the usual duties of raising a child and caring for them. They became go-betweens, spokespeople and helpers for their child's development. Parents noticed that their child depended heavily on them. They described a relationship built on watching, guessing what the child needed before it was asked, and adjusting again and again to how the child responded:

"You feel that your child really needs you for everything" (P2).

Parents' stories show a close, constant relationship in which parents are central to their child's daily support. Care is continuous, and parents are directly involved in meeting their child's needs. Parents themselves described this bond as stronger and different from the one they had with other children.

3.2.2

Subtheme 2.2: Reorganizing daily life

Parents described big changes in how family life was organized, both while they were getting the diagnosis and after. These included planning household activities and routines in detail. The reorganization showed up in constant planning of time and in adjusting how the family worked together to fit the child's needs:

"Our lives revolve largely around their highly structured daily routines" (P9).

Parents said that routine is central to how they work each day, and that it is the base on which daily activities are built. Regular tasks, such as going out, free time and family events, depend on being predictable and steady, which the child needs:

"Practically every afternoon is planned" (P5).

Parents had to plan ahead for situations that might upset the child, so they were always on alert.

"We try to anticipate everything to prevent crises, and that means we are constantly on alert" (P4).

Parents' stories show that this planning ahead reaches beyond the main activities of the day. It covers many parts of life, including schedules, travel and changes in the surroundings. Parents also said they had less room for spontaneity and took part less in social activities, which left the family somewhat cut off from others.

3.2.3

Subtheme 2.3: Effects on brothers and sisters and on the family as a whole

Parents described how having a child with ASD affects the way the whole family works together. They pointed to brothers and sisters as a group especially affected. They noticed that these siblings tended to grow up early and take on extra responsibilities. This shows up in how time, attention and responsibilities are shared at home:

"Sometimes siblings are the ones who are forgotten, and they suffer as well. We have less time for them because most of our time is devoted to caring for their sibling with ASD" (P7).

Parents said it was hard to share time and attention among family members because the child with ASD needed such specific care and support. This affected how family time was organized and how much time parents had for other children. Parents felt guilty about this unequal sharing of time and attention. They also described the need to create separate spaces for the siblings, so that each child could still have moments of attention of their own within the family:

"We try to find time just for him, but it is often difficult to do so in everyday life" (P9).

Parents' stories also show a lasting worry about the role siblings might play in the future. This worry is tied to making sure care continues, and to knowing that siblings can learn about their younger brother's or sister's needs:

"If we're ever gone, they'll have to know how to help their sister" (P6).

These accounts show that the diagnosis changed how parents shared their attention, what responsibilities family members took on, and what parents expected about future care.

3.2.4

Subtheme 2.4: Ways of coping and actively adjusting as a family

Across parents' accounts, coping came up as a mix of several things working together: setting goals that could change, actively looking for help, and slowly adjusting expectations. Instead of aiming for set results in their child's development, some parents described staying committed to their child's progress while changing their goals to fit the child's abilities and situation:

"We will go as far as we can, and once we reach that point, we will continue working" (P2).

Parents also described actively reaching out to official services to meet their child's needs and to reduce the demands on the family. This included looking for specialized services and arranging personal assistants at different times of day:

"We try to arrange as many hours of personal assistance as possible, in the morning and in the afternoon. In other words, we try to do everything we can" (P7).

These strategies worked alongside other ways of coping that came up in the earlier themes. These included asking other families for advice, creating predictable routines, planning ahead for situations that might cause distress, and slowly rethinking expectations. Together, these responses were practical, relational and about meaning. Through them, parents tried to balance their child's needs, the running of everyday family life, and their worries about the future.

However, parents did not feel that these strategies always protected them. The constant search for help, and the need to organize a lot of support, took a great deal of effort from parents. It also showed how little guidance official services gave. So coping was a process that kept changing and depended on the situation, rather than a final answer to the emotional and practical demands that come with a diagnosis.

Taken together, these accounts suggest that routines, planning ahead, speaking up for the child and setting flexible goals were not just practical answers to everyday demands. They were also ways of bringing back predictability and parents' sense of control in a situation that felt uncertain and poorly supported.

3.3

Theme 3: Worries about the future

3.3.1

Subtheme 3.1: Worrying about whether care will continue

Worry about the future was a central part of what parents said. It came up again and again, in every part of the conversation, especially about whether care would continue if the parents were no longer there. Parents repeated this worry throughout the interviews, and it became a lasting concern in their family life:

"The biggest worry is what will happen when we're gone" (P1).

Parents described this uncertainty as a central part of their daily lives. It was tied to the need to make sure that, in the future, someone else could understand their child's needs and meet them. In this sense, parents' stories show that they saw themselves as the main people who understood their child, especially when it came to communication, routines and how the child responds to everyday situations:

"You feel like you're their only voice. You wonder who will interpret their needs when you're no longer there" (P8).

Some parents described this worry in physical and emotional terms, talking about body reactions they had when they thought about the future. Uncertainty about future care is also tied to not knowing what support will be available in the long run, and to the need to plan for different possible situations:

"Sometimes you think about the future and feel a tightness in your chest, because you know that society is not prepared to care for them as we do at home" (P5).

This fear went beyond practical matters. It had an emotional side that parents saw as linked to their child possibly being vulnerable without the family home. Parents said they were still unsure about whether care would continue, whether someone would understand their child's needs, and whether support would be available in the future.

3.3.2

Subtheme 3.2: The puzzle of independence

Parents described their child's independence as an important goal in everyday life, linked to slowly building skills that help the child do more things on their own. Many parents shared this wish, tied to the hope that their child could manage on their own in different situations:

"We try to make sure that he's as independent as possible" (P3).

"We are concerned about their future employment and independence" (P10).

However, parents pointed out that this goal has to go hand in hand with adjusting expectations to the child's pace and abilities. Here, independence is not a single, fixed target. Instead, it is a gradual process that changes from one situation to another:

"Not setting fixed expectations, other than letting the child continue progressing to the level they are capable of" (P6).

"You learn to value progress that might seem small to others" (P10).

Some parents described situations where trying to push their child to learn something could upset the child.

"Sometimes I think I might have focused too much, the child has to write. In the end, you keep adding bits and pieces and it can stress them out" (P8).

These experiences show how parents kept watching their child and adjusting their expectations and demands to fit the child's responses. In this setting, parents stressed how important it was to avoid rigid expectations that might be hard for the child to meet.

"If not, we can sometimes fall into the trap of trying to frustrate the child with our expectations. That scares me a lot" (P3).

Parents described a process in which helping their child become independent went hand in hand with constantly adjusting expectations to the child's abilities and responses. It was a balance that kept shifting as parents worked to help their child become more independent.

3.3.3

Subtheme 3.3: Gaps in support as the child grows up

Parents spoke of a lasting worry about whether help and services would be available after the child finished compulsory schooling. This anxiety seems to be linked to the feeling that services shrink once a person becomes an adult:

"The future scares me because it sometimes seems that, once they turn 18, they disappear from the administration's radar" (P2).

Parents saw a clear difference between the support available while the child was at school and the support available as an adult. They also said it was unclear what options would be open after school ended. Parents worried about whether their child would have the chance to work:

"Where will they work? Who will give them a chance knowing that they need different timings?" (P14).

Parents described the need to keep actively looking for help and support, both now and in the future.

"We try to arrange as many hours of personal assistance as possible, in the morning and in the afternoon. In other words, we try to do everything we can" (P7).

This effort shows up in planning services, organizing support and looking for other options that let care continue. Some parents also stressed how important it is to reach specialized services early, so that future development can be helped through therapy, educational support and other ways of working with the child.

"We try to access the best resources now so that tomorrow will be less difficult." (P8).

Parents described feeling unsure about the support available as adults, and about the need for parents to stay involved to make sure support continues over time.

Behind these worries was not only uncertainty about whether future services would exist. Parents also feared that, without them there, their child's needs might no longer be understood, interpreted or properly supported.
parts.discussion:
4

Discussion

In this study, we set out to explore what Spanish parents lived through while their child was working through the process of getting an ASD diagnosis. We wanted to know what they expected, how they saw the way family life was reorganized as a result, and what they worried about the future. Parents' accounts suggest that an ASD diagnosis is more than a medical label. It is part of a complicated change in the family. That change brings a long period of uncertainty, disrupts everyday life, and slowly leads to adjustment. Parents adjust by speaking up for their child and by accepting neurodiversity, the idea that people's brains work in different ways and that these differences are a natural part of being human.

Across the three themes, parents described a long and uncertain journey to diagnosis and mixed feelings. They described how their expectations were reshaped step by step, how they organized everyday routines more and more carefully, how their roles as parents grew, how they saw the effects on their brothers and sisters, and how they kept worrying about future support. Taken together, these findings suggest that parents did not see the diagnosis as a single medical event. They saw it as part of a wider reorganization of everyday family life.

We therefore organize this discussion around the three themes that came out of the interviews, which we present in the Results: the journey to diagnosis and how parents adjusted; coping and the reorganization of family life; and worries about the future. We use other research, both studies and theories, to help explain our findings. We do not use it as evidence for any extra themes that we found in our own study.

When we compare our results with recent research, we see that the heavy load of daily care, and the barriers parents met in health care, education and social care, closely match what has been described for other serious conditions that affect how the brain develops in childhood. The journey to diagnosis, the load of daily care, and barriers built into the way services and health care are organized all have a deep effect. They affect not only the child but also how the whole family works and the parents' mental health (García-Bravo et al., 2023; Garcia-Bravo et al., 2025; Mackley et al., 2018; Crellin et al., 2023; Willmen et al., 2021; Jeffrey et al., 2021). Bringing these views together helps us describe the main problems in the system. It also helps us describe the strategies needed to help health care, education and social care services work together better.

Parents in our study described a "diagnostic odyssey", a long, winding journey to diagnosis. Their early suspicions often clashed with health care professionals who played down their worries or did not take them seriously, especially in primary care, the first point of contact with the health system, such as a family doctor. Parents watched their child very closely, trusting their own feelings, but no one checked or confirmed what they saw. This created a period of not knowing, which delayed the child getting help early on. These results agree with those of García-Bravo et al. (2023), who described the tensions between professionals and parents. They point out that when professionals do not actively listen during the first visits, it takes longer to reach a diagnosis, and families also lose trust in the health care system.

Parents' reports of their worries being played down and of their child being recognized late match earlier research. That research found barriers in the system that keep ASD assessments from happening in time. These include too few specialists and too little training among primary care professionals (Mathur et al., 2026). We did not look directly at these particular barriers in our study, so we use them to help explain parents' accounts, not to add to them.

Our findings more directly support the need for three things when the diagnosis is given: clear communication, delivered at a pace parents can follow; clear information about what comes next; and easy-to-use ways to be referred to services after the diagnosis. Parents described feeling shocked and lost in the system. So emotional support should also be available to parents, and care after the diagnosis should not be limited to the child alone (Daniels et al., 2021; García-Bravo et al., 2023).

Parents described getting the diagnosis as an event with deeply mixed feelings. Shock and sadness came together with relief, because they finally had an explanation for the differences they had seen in their child's development. These accounts match the change from "parent" to "expert" described by Edwards et al. (2018). Parents felt lost in the system and had no clear path to follow after the diagnosis. So they took on a more and more active role. They looked for help, reached out for support and spoke up for their children, while slowly reshaping the expectations they had had about their child's development and about family life.

We did not collect the year or date of each diagnosis. This means we could not look at how long it had been since the diagnosis, either to understand the setting or to compare parents with one another. So our study cannot tell whether differences in parents' accounts were linked to the time since diagnosis, to the child's age or support needs, to family circumstances, or to parents' experiences with services.

Even so, both the worries parents described again and again and earlier research warn against assuming that grief simply fades in a straight line as time passes. Uncertainty and feelings of loss may come back when the child moves to the next stage of life or to new services (Bravo-Benítez et al., 2019; Coughlin and Sethares, 2017; Mihandoust et al., 2021). In this way, parents' experiences resemble what researchers call "ambiguous loss" and "chronic sorrow". In ambiguous loss, a person is still there and still valued, but something about them has changed in a way that is hard to understand. Chronic sorrow is a long-lasting, recurring grief. Here, the child is still present and valued, while parents keep reshaping the expectations they had imagined for their child's development, independence and family life (Boss, 1999; O'Brien, 2007; Coughlin and Sethares, 2017).

Adjustment should therefore not be seen as the final end of grief. Instead, it is an ability that keeps growing: the ability to make the diagnosis part of family life while dealing with new challenges and new steps in the child's life. These findings support the need for services after the diagnosis that do not limit emotional support to the moment the diagnosis is given. Professionals should recognize that parents may need different kinds of information, of having their feelings confirmed, and of psychological support at each new stage of the child's life. This is especially true when worries about school, independence, adulthood and whether care will continue come back.

Parents described getting the diagnosis as an important turning point, but caring for their child did not start with the diagnosis. Before the diagnosis, parents were already watching their child's development closely, looking for explanations and again and again asking professionals to take their worries seriously. Other studies that brought together parents' accounts of the journey to diagnosis have found the same path (Boshoff et al., 2019; Smith-Young et al., 2025).

Looking back, parents described these efforts as becoming more organized and more focused on the future once the diagnosis came. This included choosing what help to get, finding their way through services, coordinating support, organizing routines, speaking up for their child, and slowly adjusting their expectations. This change matches what Edwards et al. (2018) found: parents' decision-making grew over time as they moved from being a "parent" to becoming an "expert" on their child's needs. Getting the diagnosis may therefore be better understood as reshaping and deepening the care parents were already doing, rather than creating a completely new way of caring.

Still, parents' accounts looked back on the past, and our study was not designed to follow families over time or to compare the same families before and after the diagnosis. So this explanation should be seen as an early, exploratory idea, not as proof of cause and effect.

Studies of parents of children with other conditions that affect how the brain develops in childhood have described similar experiences. These include uncertainty about the diagnosis, parents speaking up again and again, and mixed feelings (García-Bravo et al., 2023; Garcia-Bravo et al., 2025). These similarities help place our findings within the wider challenges of finding a diagnosis and getting support after it. However, they should not be read as meaning that these conditions bring the same experiences, the same path through health care, or the same support needs.

Parents' accounts show that raising a child with ASD can greatly reorganize family life and relationships. Our findings about very organized routines, heavy involvement by parents, and effects on brothers and sisters match evidence that parents and caregivers often have higher levels of depression, long-lasting stress and anxiety (Sánchez Amate and Luque de la Rosa, 2024). Professionals have also noticed that, in some cultures, spiritual beliefs or stigma (negative attitudes and unfair treatment) linked to conditions that affect how the brain develops may lead to families being cut off from others, or may delay their search for support. At the same time, parents may be exposed to conflicting information through social media and artificial intelligence. This may add to confusion and to stress in their lives and relationships, especially among parents with more education (Lotfi et al., 2026).

We can also look at these changes through a "family systems" view, which sees a family as a whole made up of members who affect one another. Seen this way, the reorganization parents described went beyond changes in routines and in the amount of care needed. Parents felt that the journey to diagnosis, and their child's ongoing support needs, affected several relationships in the home that depend on one another. These included the relationship between parent and child, the roles of the parents, and the relationships between brothers and sisters. Parents took on more duties. They became their child's voice, explained their child's needs, and coordinated support. As a result, the line between ordinary parenting and managing care became blurrier.

At the same time, the time and attention focused on the child with ASD affected brothers and sisters. Parents felt that their other children got less one-to-one attention, grew up earlier, and in some cases might end up taking on support duties in the future. These accounts can be read as showing how a change affecting one family member may be linked to adjustments across the wider family and within its different parts (Cox and Paley, 1997; Rogers et al., 2022).

Our findings also show a tension between the expectations parents had before the diagnosis and the roles and family paths that appeared afterward. Parents reshaped their expectations not only about their child's development and independence, but also about how the family takes part in life, about relationships between brothers and sisters, and about future care. Their efforts to keep special time for their other children suggest they were actively trying to balance competing needs in the home. Even so, parents worried that their other children might one day have to take on care duties. This shows that family roles and boundaries keep being worked out and renegotiated throughout the family's life. This view fits with modern family systems approaches. These approaches stress that how a family works comes from the changing interactions between individual people, their relationships, the stages of development they go through, and the society and culture around them. It does not come from the experience of any single family member on their own (Rogers et al., 2022).

However, this family systems view should be kept in mind given what we actually studied. Our findings come from the accounts of individual parents, not from interviews with couples or whole families. So the changes parents described in family roles, relationships between brothers and sisters, routines and expectations are how parents saw family life. They should not be read as a formal study of the family as a whole, or as an experience shared by everyone in the home. We were not able to check whether mothers, fathers, brothers and sisters, and other family members agreed, disagreed or differed from one another.

We want to stress that this kind of care falls mostly on women and is shaped by gender bias. As other research suggests, mothers usually become the main caregivers. This often leads them to cut back their working hours or give up their careers, which makes them less financially independent and shrinks their social network (Muiño Tato, 2026). However, two things stand out as important protective factors that can reduce emotional overload and improve family life. The first is adaptive coping, which here means positive reappraisal: looking at a hard situation in a more positive way. The second is dyadic adjustment, meaning the quality of the relationship between the two parents (García-Bravo et al., 2023; Muiño Tato, 2026).

Parents' reports of looking for services, coordinating support, speaking up for their children and adjusting their goals for their child's development match the change from "parent" to "expert" described by Edwards et al. (2018). In our study, this change showed up in three ways. Parents gained knowledge through experience. They actively found their way through services that were broken into separate pieces. And they kept adjusting their expectations to fit their child's abilities and responses. This process was closely tied to the tension between helping their child become independent and avoiding demands that were too rigid or might cause distress.

Beyond the emotional impact of the diagnosis, we found several coping strategies that were linked to one another. Parents looked for informal support from other families. They set up organized routines to make daily life more predictable. They thought ahead about situations that might cause distress. They actively searched for services. And they slowly reshaped their expectations to fit their child's own path of development. These responses combined coping through relationships, coping through practical steps, and coping by finding meaning. In particular, support from other parents, and looking positively at expectations parents had imagined for their child, match the strategies highlighted by Sánchez Amate and Luque de la Rosa (2024). They stress that social support and positive reappraisal may help protect family wellbeing.

However, these strategies should not be seen as protective in every case, or as proof that the demands of care had been solved. Routines and planning ahead helped parents make everyday family life more stable, but they also meant constant watchfulness and less room for spontaneity. In the same way, speaking up for their child and searching for resources helped parents get support, but it often came up as a response to guidance from services that was broken into pieces. Coping was therefore a changing process that depended on the situation. Through it, parents tried to balance their child's needs, how the family as a whole was working, and their own changing expectations.

Worries about the future were a separate finding, not just a continuation of today's care demands. Parents feared whether their child's communication and support needs would still be understood if they were not there. They worried whether services would still be available after the child finished compulsory schooling, and whether their child would have real chances to become independent and get a job. These accounts support the need for transition planning, which prepares for the move from school to adult life. This planning should start before the end of schooling and coordinate education, health care, social care and job-related services through the teenage years and into adulthood. However, our study did not check whether particular adult services actually existed, were easy to reach, or worked well. So these findings show how parents saw uncertainty and gaps in care. They are not an objective assessment of Spain's support system (Autismo España, 2024; Garcia-Bravo et al., 2025).

4.1

Limitations and ideas for future research

Our study gives a deep look into parents' lived experiences and how they saw the effect of an ASD diagnosis on family life, but it has several limitations. We deliberately chose to recruit parents in Spain, and most of them were mothers. This may limit how well our findings apply to other societies and cultures, and to other kinds of families. Because so few fathers took part, we could not make a meaningful comparison between mothers' and fathers' accounts. So we recorded each parent's gender, but we did not use it to group the data. Also, because parents looked back on the past, their accounts may be affected by recall bias, meaning that memories can be imperfect.

We did not collect the year or date of each diagnosis as a standard piece of information about each parent. So we could neither describe how long it had been since the diagnosis for the group as a whole nor use it to understand the setting or to compare parents. We also did not ask parents, in a matching way, to describe how they cared for their child before and after the diagnosis. As a result, parents' accounts of the past do not let us say that the diagnosis alone caused changes in parents' roles, family routines, coping strategies or the way they looked for support, either in time or in cause and effect. Nor can our study tell whether differences between parents' accounts were linked to the time since diagnosis, rather than to the child's age or support needs, to family circumstances, or to parents' experiences with services.

Getting the diagnosis may have reshaped or deepened care duties that had already started before the diagnosis. But our study was cross-sectional, meaning it looked at each family at one point in time. This does not let us work out the direction, size or timing of these changes. So our findings should not be read as a side-by-side reconstruction of how families worked before and after the diagnosis, or as evidence that every family went through the same change over time.

Each parent took part and was studied on their own, not the family as a whole. Because we did not interview couples or whole families, our findings reflect individual parents' accounts of the journey to diagnosis and how they saw its effects on family life. We did not hear directly from partners, brothers and sisters, or other caregivers. So we could not check whether family members in the same home agreed, disagreed or differed. We used a family systems view in the Discussion, but our findings should not be understood as a formal study of the family as a whole or of couples. In particular, what we found about brothers and sisters' experiences and expected duties reflects how parents saw things, not the brothers and sisters' own accounts.

Future research should recruit people from a wider range of social and economic backgrounds and cultures, and should include more kinds of families. Future studies that look at one point in time should collect and report the date or year of the diagnosis. Where it makes sense, they should also deliberately include parents at different points after the diagnosis, to see how accounts may differ over time. Studies that follow families over time, starting before the diagnosis and collecting information again and again, would help show how parents' roles, ways of caring, family routines, coping strategies and support needs change along the journey to diagnosis (Audulv et al., 2022). Studies that interview couples, or that gather information from mothers, fathers, brothers and sisters and other important caregivers, would also let researchers see how experiences, expectations and duties are worked out between different members of the family. Studies that combine interviews with measurements taken over time, of parents' wellbeing, how the family works and support needs, could add to this. Together, these approaches could build a fuller, fairer and family-centered understanding of care for conditions that affect how the brain develops.
